questions.question: The help page of `sd()` shows the usage line `sd(x, na.rm = FALSE)`. Which statement about calling `sd()` is correct?
options: Both arguments must be given in every call, because the usage line lists two arguments.
`na.rm` may be left out, and missing values in `x` are then removed automatically.
`x` has no default and must be given; `na.rm` may be left out and is then `FALSE`.
`x` may be left out, because the first argument of a function always has a default.

questions.question: When a call mixes `name = value` arguments with unnamed values, how does R decide which formal argument each unnamed value goes to?
options: It matches the named arguments first and then gives the unnamed values to the remaining formal arguments in the order of the definition.
It counts the position of each value in the call, named ones included, and gives the value in place $k$ to the $k$-th formal argument.
It looks at the type of each unnamed value, so a number goes to a numeric argument and a string to an argument that expects text.
It fills the formal arguments with the unnamed values from left to right first and then lets each named value overwrite its slot.

questions.question: The usage line of `cor()` contains `method = c("pearson", "kendall", "spearman")`. For two numeric vectors `a` and `b` of equal length, what does `cor(a, b)` compute?
options: All three correlations, returned together as a vector of length 3.
Only the Pearson correlation, as the first choice listed is used.
Only the Spearman correlation, as the last choice listed is used.
Nothing: R stops until `method` is set to one of the choices.

questions.question: Which line prints only the argument list of `cor()` with its default values, starting with `function (x, y = NULL, use = "everything"`?
options: `?cor`
`cor()`
`cor`
`args(cor)`

questions.question: What does `seq(0, 12, 3)` return?
options: an error, since only the first two arguments may be unnamed

questions.question: A student wants 7.2649 rounded to two decimals and types `round(2, 7.2649)`. What does R return?
options: an error, since `digits` must be a whole number

questions.question: Vectors `a` and `b` of equal length contain some `NA` values. Used to `mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)`, a student runs `cor(a, b, na.rm = TRUE)`. What happens?
options: R drops the incomplete pairs and returns the correlation of the rest.
R stops with the error `unused argument (na.rm = TRUE)`.
R ignores the unknown argument without a message and returns `NA`.
R returns `NA` with the warning `unused argument (na.rm = TRUE)`.

questions.question: The usage line of `log()` is `log(x, base = exp(1))`. What happens when R runs `log(base = 10)`?
options: R prints `[1] 1`, as the empty `x` copies the value of `base`.
R prints `[1] 2.302585`, as a lone value is always taken as `x`.
R stops with an error, as a named argument may not come first.
R stops with an error, as `x` has no default and is left empty.

questions.question: `log(x = 81, base = 3)` returns `[1] 4`. Which of these calls returns a different value?
options: `log(base = 3, x = 81)`
`log(81, base = 3)`
`log(base = 81, 3)`

questions.question: The usage line of `round()` is `round(x, digits = 0)`. What does `round(5.678)` return?
options: an error, since `digits` was not supplied

questions.question: After `log(8, base = 2)` has returned `[1] 3`, a student runs `log(8)`. Which statement about this second call is correct?
options: It returns `[1] 3`, as R keeps the base given in the call before it.
It returns `[1] 2.079442`, as `base` is back at its default `exp(1)`.
It returns `[1] 0.90309`, as `log()` with no base uses base 10.
It fails, as a base set once must be given again in later calls.

questions.question: The usage line of `cor()` is `cor(x, y = NULL, use = "everything", method = c("pearson", "kendall", "spearman"))`. For numeric vectors `a` and `b`, why does `cor(a, b, "spearman")` not give their Spearman correlation?
options: R reads `"spearman"` as a third data vector, and `cor()` accepts only two of them.
A string is skipped during matching, so `method` keeps its default and Pearson is used.
The third unnamed value fills the third formal argument, `use`, which rejects `"spearman"`.
`method` can only be set by name, because its default lists several choices.

questions.question: The formal arguments of `seq()` begin with `from`, `to`, `by`, `length.out`, in this order. What does `seq(5, by = 2, length.out = 4)` return?
options: the error `argument "to" is missing, with no default`

questions.question: A student wants the labels `"a" "a" "b" "b"` and writes `rep(c("a", "b"), 2)`. What does R return?
options: an error, as `rep()` cannot tell whether 2 means `times` or `each`

questions.question: `args(read.csv)` prints a line beginning `function (file, header = TRUE, sep = ",", ...`. A file `prices.csv` separates its values with semicolons. Which call reads it correctly?
options: `read.csv("prices.csv", ";")`
`read.csv(sep = ";")`
`read.csv("prices.csv", sep == ";")`
`read.csv("prices.csv", sep = ";")`

questions.question: The usage line of `cor()` includes `use = "everything"`. What does `a <- c(1, 2, NA, 4); b <- c(2, 4, 6, 8); c(cor(a, b), cor(a, b, use = "complete.obs"))` return?
options: `[1] NA NA`

questions.question: A student sees that `cor(a, b)` and `cor(b, a)` give the same value for two numeric vectors and concludes that the order of unnamed arguments never matters in R. How should this conclusion be judged?
options: Wrong: correlation is symmetric in its two inputs, while `log(8, 2)` gives 3 and `log(2, 8)` gives 0.3333333.
Right: R matches unnamed values to formal arguments by type, so two numeric vectors can be given in any order.
Right whenever both calls run, since R warns when it receives unnamed values in an unexpected order.
Wrong: swapping `a` and `b` always changes the sign, so `cor(b, a)` equals minus `cor(a, b)`.

questions.question: The help pages give the usage lines `median(x, na.rm = FALSE, ...)` and `mean(x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE, ...)`, and `mean()` stops with an error when `trim` is not a number. For `v <- c(4, NA, 8, 6)`, what do `median(v, TRUE)` and `mean(v, TRUE)` do?
options: Both return `[1] 6`, since `TRUE` given second means `na.rm = TRUE`.
Both return `[1] NA`, since `na.rm` only works when written by name.
`median(v, TRUE)` returns `[1] 6`; `mean(v, TRUE)` returns `[1] NA`.
`median(v, TRUE)` returns `[1] 6`; `mean(v, TRUE)` stops with an error.

questions.question: To print $\sqrt{10}$ rounded to two decimals, a student types `round(sqrt(10, 2))`. What happens?
options: R prints `[1] 3.16`, since the 2 is passed on to `round()`.
R stops at `sqrt()`, which takes only one argument.
R prints `[1] 3`, since `sqrt()` drops the 2 and `round()` uses 0.
R stops at `round()`, which needs `digits` to be given.

questions.question: With `log(x, base = exp(1))` as the definition of `log()`, what is the outcome of the call `log(100, 10, base = 2)`?
options: R prints `[1] 2`.
R stops: `unused argument (10)`.
R stops: `formal argument "base" matched by multiple actual arguments`.
